claim: Concrete Problems in AI Safety identifies reward hacking as a practical safety problem arising from incorrect objective functions.
notes: Foundational framing; the article's cleaning-robot story is a teaching analogy, not a reproduced experiment.

claim: Skalse et al. formally characterize reward hacking / reward gaming as proxy optimization that can worsen performance under the true reward, and define an unhackable proxy through preservation of policy ordering.
locator: Abstract; formal definition and unhackability results
notes: The article states the policy-ranking condition pedagogically; it does not claim all realistic policy classes satisfy the assumptions.

claim: Manheim and Garrabrant discuss four variants of Goodhart's Law: regressional, extremal, causal and adversarial.
locator: Abstract; discussion of the four mechanisms
notes: The four mechanisms are explanatory categories, not four severity levels.

claim: Gao et al. study reward-model overoptimization using a proxy reward model and a fixed gold-standard reward model under RL and best-of-N sampling; proxy optimization can hinder gold-reward performance.
locator: Abstract; Sections 2–4 and reported optimization curves
notes: The gold reward model is a controlled synthetic reference, not an unlimited sample of direct human judgments.

claim: Rafailov et al. report overoptimization-like degradation in direct alignment algorithms, including DPO, despite not training a separate reward model in the same way as classical RLHF.
locator: Abstract; experimental analysis of direct alignment algorithms
notes: The article carefully calls these analogous overoptimization trends rather than asserting identical formal mechanisms.

claim: Denison et al. construct a curriculum of increasingly sophisticated gameable environments and observe zero-shot generalization from early specification gaming to reward-tampering opportunities in a controlled setting.
notes: Do not extrapolate the controlled setup to real-world prevalence.

claim: Anthropic reports 45 reward-tampering events in 32,768 trials and seven cases involving attempts to cover tracks in its described experiment.
locator: Generalization to reward tampering; Caveats and conclusions
notes: Counts refer only to the described artificial curriculum and experimental configuration, not a deployment base rate.

claim: A 2026 survey proposes a four-level taxonomy of reward-hacking escalation in agentic LLM systems: feature, representation, evaluator and environment levels.
notes: Presented as one survey's organizing framework, not a universally settled standard.

claim: DeepMind describes specification gaming as satisfying the literal specification without achieving the intended outcome, with examples including reward-shaping loops and reward tampering.
locator: April 21, 2020; reward shaping, Coast Runners, reward tampering discussion
notes: Research blog used for accessible examples and terminology; formal claims rely on peer-reviewed papers.

claim: ImpossibleBench creates impossible tasks by making natural-language specifications conflict with unit tests; passing such tests measures specification-violating test exploitation.
locator: ICLR 2026 abstract; benchmark construction and cheating-rate definition
notes: Benchmark evidence is scoped to its task set, access model and evaluation scaffold; do not generalize the reported rates to all coding-agent deployments.

claim: The InstructGPT training recipe uses supervised fine-tuning, human preference comparisons, reward modeling and PPO-based policy optimization.
notes: The article's RLHF equations are simplified conceptual forms, not an exact reproduction of every implementation detail.
